## The question

\vspace{1.5em}

\begin{center}
\Large\bfseries\color{econblue}
How should we compute the standard suite of climate indices\\[0.1em]
from daily observations in a single reproducible R interface?
\end{center}

\vspace{1em}

\begin{center}
\normalsize\itshape
Thirty indices, five families, one consistent tidy output schema.
\end{center}

::: notes
Open with the question, not the package. The problem: climate-index
analysis is routine but the R ecosystem delivers it piecemeal. We need
a single interface that matches the way analysts actually work.
:::


## Why it matters

- **National statistical offices** publish annual climate-index tables
- **Agricultural research** tracks growing-season and heliothermal indices
- **Insurance underwriters** price parametric drought and heat products
- **Public-health authorities** monitor heat-index exceedances in real time

::: notes
Four distinct stakeholder groups, four live use cases. Point at
insurance and public health: those are the fastest-growing demand
segments. 60 seconds.
:::



## What is already out there

- **`SPEI`**: drought indices only, narrow scope\footnote{\scriptsize Begueria \& Vicente-Serrano (2017), \textit{SPEI: Calculation of the Standardised Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index}, R package v1.7.}
- **`climdex.pcic`**: standard ETCCDI indices, archived on CRAN
- **`Evapotranspiration`, various agri packages**: fragmented, inconsistent output schemas
- **Station-level tooling**: bespoke scripts, no reusable public interface

\vspace{0.5em}

The gap: **no single package unifies the standard workflow with a tidy output schema**.

::: notes
Respect existing packages. climdex.pcic covered the same ground for a
decade but is now archived. climatekit fills the vacuum. 45 seconds.
:::



## What climatekit offers

1. **Coverage**: 30+ indices across 5 families (temperature, precipitation, drought, agroclimatology, thermal comfort)
2. **Interface**: every function returns the same four-column tidy schema; outputs compose via `rbind()`
3. **Provenance**: pure computation, no API calls, no network dependency, 133 unit tests

\vspace{0.5em}

On CRAN since March 2026. Definitions follow ETCCDI recommendations\footnote{\scriptsize Zhang et al.\ (2011), \textit{Indices for monitoring changes in extremes based on daily temperature and precipitation data}, WIREs Climate Change 2(6).}.

::: notes
Three bullets, three selling points. Emphasise the tidy schema: that is
the usability advantage. CRAN presence signals maturity. 45 seconds.
:::

## Central formulas

\vspace{0.3em}

\textbf{Frost days} (count below $0^{\circ}$C):
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{FD} = \sum_t \mathbf{1}\!\left\{T_{\min,t} < 0^\circ\mathrm{C}\right\}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Growing degree days} (cumulative heat above base $b$):
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{GDD}_b = \sum_t \max\!\left(T_{\mathrm{mean},t} - b,\ 0\right)
\end{equation}

\textbf{Standardised Precipitation Index} (McKee et al. 1993):
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{SPI}_s = \Phi^{-1}\!\left[F(P_s;\ \alpha, \beta)\right]
\end{equation}

::: notes
Three equations, one family each. Do not read them aloud. Point at the
indicator function in FD and the gamma CDF in SPI. The pattern across
indices is: simple rule applied consistently across daily observations.
60 seconds.
:::



## Package at a glance

::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}

Function families:

- **Temperature**: 8 functions
- **Precipitation**: 7 functions
- **Drought** (SPI, SPEI, PET): 3 functions
- **Agroclimatology** (Huglin, Winkler, Branas): 5 functions
- **Thermal comfort**: 4 functions
- **Dispatchers**: `ck_compute()`, `ck_available()`, `ck_metadata()`

Deps: `cli`, `stats`, `tools`. R $\geq$ 4.1.0.

:::
::: {.column width="40%"}

\begin{block}{Uniform output}
Every function returns:

\texttt{period} | \texttt{value} | \texttt{index} | \texttt{unit}

Outputs compose via \texttt{rbind()} into panel data.
\end{block}

:::
:::

::: notes
Two columns. Left lists the families. Right highlights the output
schema in the blue block. The consistency is the pitch. 45 seconds.
:::



## Minimal working example

```r
library(climatekit)

# Three indices from Central Park daily observations
fd   <- ck_frost_days(tmin,  dates, period = "annual")
gdd  <- ck_gdd(tmin, tmax,   dates, base = 10, period = "annual")
spi3 <- ck_spi(precip,       dates, scale = 3)

# Compose into a panel for plotting or modelling
panel <- rbind(fd, gdd, spi3)
```

\footnotesize
All three calls share the same four-column schema, so `rbind()` works
without reshaping or renaming.

::: notes
Live-read the code. Three calls, three data frames, one rbind. That is
the entire user experience. No data-frame wrangling, no column
conformance. 60 seconds.
:::



## Central Park temperature trends, 1950 to 2024

**Data.** NOAA GHCND station USW00094728. 75 years of daily $T_{\min}$, $T_{\max}$, and precipitation. Complete record through 2024.

**Question.** *How have temperature indices evolved in the US Northeast over seven decades?*

**Why this case.** Flagship US long-record station. Northeast warming debate active in *J. Climate*\footnote{\scriptsize Brown \& DeGaetano (2013), \textit{Trends in U.S. surface humidity}, J. Applied Meteorology 52.}. Three indices with distinct signals (warming, stable, trending). Reproducible with three public function calls.

::: notes
Setup only. No results on this slide. Point forward: hero figure is
next. Name the station, the period, the question, and why Central Park
is the right station. 45 seconds.
:::

## What climatekit does not yet do

- **Daily observations only**: no sub-hourly heat-wave indices
- **No gridded input helpers**: users reduce rasters to per-cell series first
- **SPI / SPEI use gamma distribution**: Pearson III not exposed for arid regions
- **No station homogenisation**: quality control is upstream user responsibility

\vspace{0.5em}

**v0.2.0 roadmap**: hourly heat-wave indices, gridded input wrappers, additional fire-weather variants (Canadian FFMC, DC, ISI).

::: notes
Honest limitations. Name each one. Frame v0.2.0 as a commitment, not a
vague plan. The hourly heat-wave extension matters most to public
health users. 45 seconds.
:::
